Nuevo Laredo now stands as the municipality in Tamaulipas with the lowest perceived insecurity, with just 20.4% of residents feeling the city is unsafe, according to the latest results of the Encuesta Nacional de Seguridad Pública Urbana (ENSU), published by Mexico's national statistics institute, INEGI, as reported by Reporte 43.

The figure means roughly eight in ten people surveyed consider Nuevo Laredo safe to live in — a striking reversal from 2021, when perceived insecurity stood at 70.4% at the start of Mayor Carmen Lilia Canturosas Villarreal's administration, the report noted. That is a 50-percentage-point drop.

The improvement accelerated recently: Nuevo Laredo went from 26.5% in June to 20.4% in September 2026, a 6.1-point decline in a single quarter.

The results landed in a favorable national context. Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo noted Friday that nationwide perceived insecurity fell to 58.1% in September, the lowest level recorded in the 13 years since the ENSU began.

According to the report, city officials credit a strategy of coordinated work with the federal government under Sheinbaum and the Tamaulipas state government under Gov. Américo Villarreal Anaya, along with prevention programs and an approach that addresses the root causes of violence — investing in social programs, education, public works, and economic development. “Attending the causes, recovering spaces for coexistence, and generating opportunities” is part of the safety strategy, the city says.

For the municipal government, the challenge now is maintaining the trend and strengthening citizen trust through continued coordination with state and federal authorities, Reporte 43 wrote.

Sources: Reporte 43, based on INEGI ENSU results, Oct. 23, 2026.

excerpt: INEGI's latest ENSU survey puts Nuevo Laredo's perceived insecurity at just 20.4% — the lowest in Tamaulipas and down from 70.4% in 2021 — with roughly 8 in 10 residents now calling the city safe.
title: Nuevo Laredo posts Tamaulipas' lowest perceived insecurity: 8 in 10 residents feel safe
